questions.title: @OneToMany Relationship
questions.question: How do you map a @OneToMany relationship and what are the key considerations?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`mappedBy`:** names the owning side field — without it, a join table is created
- **`FetchType.LAZY` default:** always keep it — eager causes performance problems
- **Cascade types:** `PERSIST`, `MERGE`, `REMOVE`, `ALL` — understand implications of `REMOVE`
- **Bidirectional sync:** if bidirectional, maintain both sides of the relationship
- **Red flag:** not knowing `mappedBy` or using `EAGER` on collections

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A `@OneToMany` relationship maps one entity to a collection of another. The critical parameter is `mappedBy` — it tells JPA that the foreign key lives on the many side, not in a join table. Without `mappedBy`, JPA creates an unnecessary join table.

`FetchType.LAZY` is the default for `@OneToMany` and you should keep it that way. If you change it to EAGER, every query for the parent entity will join and load all children — even when you only need the parent's fields. This causes significant performance problems at scale.

For bidirectional relationships, you must keep both sides in sync. When adding an item to an order, you set `item.setOrder(order)` and also `order.getItems().add(item)`. A helper method on the parent entity — `addItem(Item item)` — keeps this in sync and prevents inconsistent state.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: A @OneToMany relationship maps one entity to a collection of another.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: A helper method on the parent entity — addItem(Item item) — keeps this in sync and prevents inconsistent state.

questions.title: @ManyToOne Relationship
questions.question: How does @ManyToOne work and what is the owning side?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@ManyToOne` is the owning side:** the foreign key column lives in this table
- **`@JoinColumn`:** specifies the FK column name
- **Default fetch type:** `EAGER` for `@ManyToOne` (opposite of `@OneToMany`)
- **Change to LAZY:** for `@ManyToOne` — avoid loading parent just to get child
- **Red flag:** not knowing `@ManyToOne` is EAGER by default and not changing it

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@ManyToOne` is the owning side of the relationship — the entity annotated with `@ManyToOne` holds the foreign key column in its table. `@JoinColumn(name = "order_id")` specifies the exact column name.

A critical and often overlooked fact: `@ManyToOne`'s default fetch type is `EAGER`, unlike `@OneToMany` which defaults to `LAZY`. This means when you load an `Item`, Hibernate automatically loads the `Order` even if you never use it. For deeply nested hierarchies, this eagerness cascades — loading the item loads the order, which might load the customer, which might load the address.

Always override to `FetchType.LAZY` on `@ManyToOne` unless you have a specific reason. This makes your queries predictable and prevents silent performance degradation.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @ManyToOne is the owning side of the relationship — the entity annotated with @ManyToOne holds the foreign key column in its table.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This makes your queries predictable and prevents silent performance degradation.

questions.title: @ManyToMany Relationship
questions.question: How do you map a @ManyToMany relationship and when should you use an intermediate entity?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@JoinTable`:** defines the join table — name, FK columns
- **`mappedBy` on inverse side:** specifies which side is the owner
- **Intermediate entity alternative:** when join table has extra columns (quantity, timestamp)
- **`Set` vs `List` for collections:** Set avoids Hibernate's duplicate handling issue
- **Red flag:** using `@ManyToMany` when the join table needs extra columns — use intermediate entity

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A `@ManyToMany` relationship requires a join table in the database. You designate one side as the owner and annotate it with `@JoinTable`, specifying the join table name and the FK columns. The other side uses `mappedBy` to reference the owner.

The important limitation: `@ManyToMany` assumes the join table has only two foreign key columns. The moment your join table needs extra columns — like a `quantity` in a product-tag relationship, or `addedAt` timestamp — you must replace `@ManyToMany` with an intermediate entity. This intermediate entity maps both foreign keys as `@ManyToOne` relationships and adds the extra columns as normal fields.

Use `Set` instead of `List` for `@ManyToMany` collections. With `List`, Hibernate's collection management deletes and reinserts all join table rows on any collection change. With `Set`, it makes surgical changes.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: A @ManyToMany relationship requires a join table in the database.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: With Set, it makes surgical changes.

questions.title: @OneToOne Relationship
questions.question: How do you map a @OneToOne relationship and what are its performance implications?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **FK can be on either side:** `@JoinColumn` on one, `mappedBy` on the other
- **Lazy loading issue with `@OneToOne`:** proxy doesn't work like `@ManyToOne` — can't be truly lazy
- **`@PrimaryKeyJoinColumn`:** share PK instead of separate FK — solves lazy issue
- **Consider merging into one entity:** if they're always loaded together
- **Red flag:** not knowing `@OneToOne` can't be truly lazy on the non-owning side

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@OneToOne` maps two entities with a one-to-one relationship. One side holds the foreign key and the other uses `mappedBy`. The unique constraint on the FK column enforces the one-to-one cardinality.

A subtle but important issue: on the non-owning side — the side with `mappedBy` — `@OneToOne(fetch = LAZY)` doesn't actually work lazily. Hibernate must issue a query to determine if the associated entity exists or is null. It can't use a proxy for null checks. This means `@OneToOne` on the inverse side is effectively always EAGER.

If lazy loading matters, use `@PrimaryKeyJoinColumn` — the two entities share the same primary key value. Or consider whether the two entities should be merged into one table — if you always load them together, a single entity with all fields is simpler and more efficient.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @OneToOne maps two entities with a one-to-one relationship.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Or consider whether the two entities should be merged into one table — if you always load them together, a single entity with all fields is simpler and more efficient.

questions.title: FetchType LAZY vs EAGER
questions.question: What is the difference between LAZY and EAGER fetching and which should you use?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **LAZY:** proxy placeholder, loads on first access
- **EAGER:** joins and loads immediately with the parent query
- **Defaults:** `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` = EAGER; `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` = LAZY
- **Always use LAZY:** override EAGER defaults on `@ManyToOne` — control loading per query
- **Red flag:** not knowing the defaults — EAGER on `@ManyToOne` catches many developers off guard

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
LAZY fetching creates a proxy object for the associated entity. The actual data is loaded from the database only when you first access a property on that proxy. EAGER fetching joins and loads the association in the same query as the parent entity — immediately, unconditionally.

The JPA defaults are: `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` are LAZY. `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` are EAGER by default — which is dangerous. EAGER on `@ManyToOne` means every query for an entity automatically joins its parent, even if you never use the parent.

The best practice is to make everything LAZY and control loading explicitly per use case with JOIN FETCH or Entity Graphs. This gives you predictable query behaviour — you know exactly what queries execute.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: LAZY fetching creates a proxy object for the associated entity.
speakable_v2.cap: This gives you predictable query behaviour — you know exactly what queries execute.

questions.title: Cascade Operations
questions.question: How do JPA cascade types work and which are safe to use?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`CascadeType.ALL` = all cascade operations:** use only when child is truly owned by parent
- **`PERSIST` + `MERGE`:** safe for parent-managed children
- **`REMOVE`:** dangerous on `@ManyToMany` — can delete shared entities
- **`orphanRemoval`:** removes children removed from the collection — different from `REMOVE`
- **Red flag:** using `CascadeType.ALL` on `@ManyToMany` — deleting one product deletes all shared tags

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Cascade types propagate JPA operations from parent to child. `PERSIST` means saving the parent also saves new children. `MERGE` means merging the parent also merges children. `REMOVE` means deleting the parent also deletes children. `ALL` applies all cascade types.

The safe cascades are `PERSIST` and `MERGE` for `@OneToMany` where children are owned by the parent — like order items. `REMOVE` and `ALL` are appropriate for child entities that make no sense without the parent — when deleting an order, delete its items too.

The dangerous combination is `CascadeType.REMOVE` (or `ALL`) on `@ManyToMany`. If you delete a `Product` and cascade removes its `Tag` entities, you might delete tags shared by other products. Only use `REMOVE` when children are exclusively owned by one parent.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Cascade types propagate JPA operations from parent to child.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Only use REMOVE when children are exclusively owned by one parent.

questions.title: @Embeddable and @Embedded
questions.question: What is @Embeddable and when should you use it?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@Embeddable`:** a value object that has no identity of its own
- **`@Embedded`:** marks the field containing the embeddable in the owner entity
- **No separate table:** embedded columns are in the parent entity's table
- **`@AttributeOverride`:** rename embedded columns when the same type is embedded twice
- **Use case:** address, money, date range — value objects

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@Embeddable` marks a class as a value object — it has no independent identity and its state is stored in the owning entity's table, not a separate table. This is perfect for domain concepts like `Address`, `Money`, or `DateRange` that are part of an entity but shouldn't be separate entities themselves.

The `@Embedded` annotation on the field in the owning entity tells JPA to embed the `@Embeddable`'s columns inline. An `Order` might have a `@Embedded Address shippingAddress` — the address columns go directly in the `orders` table: `shipping_street`, `shipping_city`, `shipping_country`.

When you embed the same type twice — like `billingAddress` and `shippingAddress` — the default column names would conflict. `@AttributeOverride` lets you rename each embedding's columns.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @Embeddable marks a class as a value object — it has no independent identity and its state is stored in the owning entity's table, not a separate table.
speakable_v2.cap: @AttributeOverride lets you rename each embedding's columns.

questions.title: Bidirectional Relationship Management
questions.question: What are the pitfalls of bidirectional relationships and how do you manage them correctly?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Both sides must be in sync:** not syncing causes inconsistent state within the same session
- **Helper methods on the owner:** `addItem()`/`removeItem()` sync both sides atomically
- **`toString()` and `equals()` cycles:** bidirectional can cause infinite recursion
- **Owning side controls persistence:** only the owning side's FK is written to the DB
- **Red flag:** only setting one side and wondering why changes aren't persisted

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
In a bidirectional relationship, JPA only writes the owning side to the database — the side without `mappedBy`. But within a session, both sides must be in sync or you'll get inconsistent state. If you add an item to `order.getItems()` but don't set `item.setOrder(order)`, the object graph is inconsistent in memory — the item doesn't know its parent.

The pattern to manage this is helper methods on the parent entity. `addItem(Item item)` adds the item to the collection AND sets `item.setOrder(this)`. `removeItem(Item item)` removes from the collection AND sets `item.setOrder(null)`. This is always done atomically through the helper.

Another pitfall is `toString()` and `equals()`: if your `Order.toString()` includes `items` and `Item.toString()` includes `order`, you get a `StackOverflowError`. Exclude bidirectional references from `toString()`, `equals()`, and `hashCode()`.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: In a bidirectional relationship, JPA only writes the owning side to the database — the side without mappedBy.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Exclude bidirectional references from toString(), equals(), and hashCode().

questions.title: @JoinColumn Configuration
questions.question: How do you configure @JoinColumn for relationship mappings?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`name`:** the FK column name in the owning entity's table
- **`referencedColumnName`:** what column on the referenced table it points to (default: PK)
- **`nullable = false`:** adds NOT NULL constraint
- **`@ForeignKey`:** name the constraint for cleaner DDL
- **Red flag:** not knowing `@JoinColumn` is only on the owning side

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`@JoinColumn` configures the foreign key column on the owning side of a relationship. The `name` attribute specifies the column name in the database. Without `@JoinColumn`, Hibernate generates a column name from the field name and referenced table name.

`referencedColumnName` specifies which column on the referenced table the FK points to — defaults to the referenced entity's primary key, which is almost always what you want. You'd override it only to join on a unique non-PK column.

`nullable = false` adds a NOT NULL constraint — important for relationships that are mandatory. Combined with `@Column(name = ...)` naming discipline, your schema DDL will be clean and explicit rather than relying on Hibernate's naming conventions.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: @JoinColumn configures the foreign key column on the owning side of a relationship.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Combined with @Column(name = ...) naming discipline, your schema DDL will be clean and explicit rather than relying on Hibernate's naming conventions.

questions.title: Collection Mapping Best Practices
questions.question: What are the best practices for mapping collections in JPA entities?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Always initialize collections:** `new ArrayList<>()` prevents NullPointerException
- **`Set` for `@ManyToMany`:** prevents Hibernate's bag duplication issue
- **`List` with `@OrderColumn`:** preserves order in the DB
- **Avoid adding to collection and expecting FK to be written:** only the owning side matters
- **Red flag:** not initializing collections — NPE when accessing lazy collection on detached entity

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Always initialize collection fields with empty collections — `new ArrayList<>()` or `new HashSet<>()`. Without initialization, you get `NullPointerException` when calling `entity.getItems().add(item)` on a new entity before it's persisted.

For `@OneToMany`, use `List` — ordering is meaningful for line items, history records, and similar sequences. For `@ManyToMany`, use `Set` — Hibernate's handling of `List` bags in many-to-many relationships deletes and reinserts all rows on any collection change, which is inefficient.

If you need a specific order persisted in the database, add `@OrderColumn` to maintain a position column in the join or child table. Without it, the database doesn't guarantee order — you'd sort in Java or via JPQL ORDER BY.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Always initialize collection fields with empty collections — new ArrayList<>() or new HashSet<>().
speakable_v2.cap: Without it, the database doesn't guarantee order — you'd sort in Java or via JPQL ORDER BY.
